body.hook: Every product you use started as a problem. Someone needed a phone stand, a better backpack strap or a bike rack that fits a small yard. Before they built anything, designers wrote down exactly what the solution had to do. That's called a design brief, and it keeps the whole project on track.

study.title: Unpack the Brief
study.question: How do designers turn a problem into a plan?
study.passage:
Design brief: "Grade 6 students in our school's reading room keep losing their place in library books and bending pages. Design a bookmark-and-book-stand combination that holds a book open at an angle on a desk. It must fold flat to fit in a backpack, be made from materials available in our CTF lab (cardboard, thin wood, fabric, string, tape and glue), cost under $3 in materials, and be built in two 60-minute classes."
Part 1, Unpack (10 minutes): Highlight the problem, user, criteria and constraints. Fill in the brief organizer.
Part 2, Criteria (10 minutes): Turn the brief into a checklist:
• Holds a book open at an angle
• Folds flat for a backpack
• Marks the page
• Uses only lab materials
• Costs under $3
• Built in two classes
Part 3, Brainstorm (10 minutes): Write or sketch as many ideas as possible in 5 minutes. No idea is too odd.
Part 4, Thumbnails (15 minutes): Choose your three best ideas and draw thumbnail sketches with labels. Then score each idea against the criteria and choose one to develop.

body.hook: Before Leonardo da Vinci built anything, he filled notebooks with quick sketches: flying machines, bridges, gears. Most were never built, but the sketches let him try dozens of ideas in minutes. Sketching is how designers think on paper.

study.title: Idea Factory
study.question: How do sketches help designers turn ideas into plans?
study.passage:
Design brief (written for this lesson): "Design a desk organizer for a Grade 8 student. It must hold at least 6 pencils, a ruler (30 cm), a phone and sticky notes; fit in a space 25 cm wide by 15 cm deep; and be made from wood, card or fabric available in the CTF room."
Part 1, Brainstorm (5 minutes): Write every idea you can think of. No idea is too strange.
Part 2, Thumbnails (10 minutes): Draw at least six thumbnail sketches, each in a box about 5 cm square. Annotate each with one strength and one weakness.
Part 3, Choose: Compare thumbnails against the brief. Star the best one.
Part 4, Orthographic drawing (20 minutes): Draw front, top and side views of your chosen idea on grid paper, lined up with each other, with all main dimensions in centimetres.

body.hook: Skateboard decks are made of maple, phone cases of silicone, sails of nylon. Each material was chosen because of how it behaves: strong, flexible, light, waterproof or cheap. Choosing the wrong material can ruin a great design.

study.title: Material Match
study.question: How do I choose the best material for my design?
study.passage:
Material testing stations (written for this lesson):
Station 1, Strength: Hang a 500 g mass from a 2 cm strip of each material. Does it hold or tear?
Station 2, Rigidity: Clamp a 15 cm strip and press the end. How far does it bend?
Station 3, Water: Drip 5 drops of water. Does it soak in, warp or stay dry?
Station 4, Workability: Can you cut and join it with tools in the CTF room? How long does it take?
Materials to test: pine strip, MDF, corrugated card, felt, canvas, recycled plastic sheet.
Cost and sustainability card: pine (medium cost, renewable), MDF (low cost, contains glue), corrugated card (very low cost, recyclable), felt (low cost), canvas (medium cost, durable), recycled plastic (medium cost, reuses waste).
Then choose the main material for your desk organizer and justify it.
